beats.say: A service runs fine for three days. Its heap rises, drops at every garbage collection, rises again. But the low point keeps creeping up. Then: out of memory error, Java heap space.
Restart it, and it's fine for three more days. Then it dies again.
So where does memory go in Java? And who is supposed to free it?
Java, part four. JVM memory, and garbage collection.
Start with where values live.
Every thread gets its own stack. Calling main pushes a frame, holding main's local variables. Here, demo: a reference to an object.

Main calls run, and a second frame goes on top. Count equals ten is stored right in the frame. But new Person creates the object on the heap, shared by every thread. P one holds its address. P two copies the address, so both point to one object.
String literals go to the String pool, inside the heap. S one and S two share one pooled string. New String always makes a fresh object, so s one equals equals s three is false.
When run returns, its frame is popped. Last in, first out. The variables are gone. But the Person object is still on the heap, with nothing pointing to it.
And if recursion never stops, frames pile up until the stack runs out: a stack overflow error.
So when is an object garbage?
A equals b. Now nothing points to object one. It looks like garbage. But that's not quite how Java decides.
The JVM starts from GC roots. Local variables in live stack frames, static fields, running threads. It follows every reference from there. Whatever it reaches is live.
Objects four and five point to each other, but no root reaches them. So both are garbage. Java doesn't count references. It traces from roots, so cycles get collected.
And System dot gc is only a hint. The JVM decides when to collect.
References also come in strengths. A normal, strong reference keeps an object alive, no matter what.
A soft reference lets the GC take the object, but only when memory runs low. Perfect for a cache.
A weak reference lets it go at the very next collection. That's how a weak hash map drops entries nobody uses.
And a phantom reference never returns the object. It only tells you it's gone, so you can clean up.
Now, how the heap is organised.
Most objects die young. A request creates thousands of little objects, and a few milliseconds later they're garbage. So the heap is split by age: a young generation, and an old one.
Every new object starts in Eden. Here are five: O one to O five.

Eden fills, and a minor GC runs. It pauses the app, finds O one, three and four still alive, and copies them into survivor space zero, with age one. Then it wipes Eden in one go. Dead objects cost nothing.
Two new objects arrive. Next minor GC: O four and O six are dead. The survivors move to survivor space one, and their ages go up. The two survivor spaces swap every time.
With a threshold of three, O one and O three have now survived three collections. They're promoted to the old generation.
The real default threshold is fifteen. And the old generation is collected less often, by a major GC, with longer pauses.
How does a collector actually free memory? First, mark: everything reachable from the roots gets marked live.
Then sweep: everything unmarked is freed. But now free space is scattered in little holes. A big array might not fit anywhere.
So compact: slide the survivors together, leaving one free block.
The young generation skips all that. It copies live objects out, and wipes the whole space.
Class metadata lives outside the heap, in metaspace. Before Java eight, it lived in a fixed size area called perm gen, which filled up and crashed app servers. Metaspace grows as needed.
Static fields and the string pool are not there. They're on the heap.
Next: which collector?
Every collector trades throughput against pauses. A stop the world pause freezes every application thread while the collector works.
Serial uses one GC thread. One long pause. Fine for tiny heaps.
Parallel uses many GC threads. Shorter pauses, the best throughput. Great for batch jobs. It was the default up to Java eight.
G1, the default since Java nine, splits the heap into regions, and keeps each pause near a target of two hundred milliseconds.
And ZGC does almost all its work while your app keeps running. Pauses under about a millisecond, even on huge heaps.
So: default to G1. Parallel for batch. ZGC for strict latency. And CMS? Removed in Java fourteen.
Here's G1's heap. Equal regions, each one Eden, survivor, old, or humongous, for very large objects.
Each pause collects the regions with the most garbage first. That's the name: garbage first. Their live objects are copied into free regions, so it compacts as it goes.
Back to the service that dies every three days.
Login puts each session into a static map. Logout never removes it. A static field is a GC root.
So every session ever created stays reachable, and the GC can never free it. The low point after each collection keeps rising, until the heap is full.
To prove it, take a heap dump, automatically on out of memory, or live with j c m d. Open it in Eclipse MAT, and the leak suspect points straight at the map.
The fix: remove on logout, and bound the cache, with a size limit or an expiry.
One more trap, in Kubernetes. A pod with a one gigabyte limit, and no heap flags. The JVM takes just a quarter of it: two hundred fifty six megabytes. Out of memory, with most of the pod unused.

Set the heap to the full gigabyte instead, and the JVM still needs memory outside the heap: metaspace, thread stacks, the code cache. The pod goes over its limit, and the kernel kills it. O O M killed. Exit code one three seven.
So set max RAM percentage to around seventy five. The heap scales with the pod, and leaves room for the rest.
Let's lock it in.
Stack frames hold locals, per thread. Every object lives on the shared heap.
Anything reachable from a GC root is live. Everything else is garbage.
A minor GC copies survivors between survivor spaces, and ages them.
Old enough, and they're promoted to the old generation.
G1 is the default: regions, and a pause target.
And a memory leak is something still reachable, that you no longer need.
Before the next part: from memory, draw Eden, the two survivor spaces, and the old generation.
Then walk five objects through three minor GCs, with a threshold of three, and write every age.
That's JVM memory. See you in part five.
